UNIT 1 / WEEK 13 / CHAPTER 13

Designing and protecting a network

Design a network for a school scenario. Show how it connects, who can use each resource, and what might limit its performance.

NETWORKS CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Distinguish LAN, WLAN and WAN.
  • Produce and explain a logical network diagram.
  • Explain security controls and network performance factors.

Before you start: Distinguish local and routed traffic, device roles and connection media.

Revisit if needed: Addresses, devices and media.

Find this chapter’s activities and downloads · Practice after reading: Design against capacity and access requirements.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. Scale and logical diagrams

A school site may use a LAN, a local area network. Its wireless part is a WLAN. A WAN connects networks over a larger geographic area. Wireless describes the connection method, not how far the network reaches.

Draw a logical diagram to show how devices connect and how communication is organised. For course diagrams, use the Cisco-style symbols in the SCSA support booklet. Label devices, links and any required IP addresses and masks. A text chain such as Internet → modem → firewall → router → switch → clients helps you plan, but does not replace those symbols.

SCSA diagram convention: place the firewall outside the trusted network and do not assign it an IP address in the assessment diagram. Real firewall deployments vary. Consult the official support booklet for the expected symbol layout.

2. Protect against unauthorised access

Start with what a user needs to do. A student may need to read a learning resource but should not need to change administrative files. Give the account only the access needed for its role. This is least privilege.

Use several controls together:

  • Use firewall rules to permit or block network traffic.
  • Keep operating systems updated and use suitable sign-in methods and account permissions.
  • Separate guest devices from school administrative resources.
  • Protect wireless access with appropriate authentication and encryption.
  • Lock devices and protect credentials.

For each control, explain which threat it reduces. A permitted connection is not automatically safe.

3. Find the bottleneck

If many users report slow downloads, first find the part limiting the transfer. This is the bottleneck. It might be an Internet link, a busy server or shared wireless airtime. Bandwidth is capacity; throughput is the transfer rate you actually achieve. Latency is delay. More capacity does not automatically remove delay.

Devices transmitting at the same time on a shared medium can cause collisions. Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet avoids the collisions of older shared half-duplex Ethernet. Wi-Fi shares radio airtime and uses collision-avoidance mechanisms.

A broadcast uses resources across its broadcast domain. Basic switching does not remove broadcasts; routers ordinarily separate broadcast domains. Before changing a design, check link use, client numbers, signal quality, service load and traffic patterns. Explain how your proposed change addresses the evidence.

Read the units: a bit is one binary digit; a byte contains 8 bits. A rate in megabits per second is not the same as megabytes per second. In a simplified calculation, transfer time = data size ÷ transfer rate. At a constant 20 megabits per second, 80 megabits takes 4 seconds. Real transfers also have overheads and delays.

Pause and predict: Would doubling the link’s advertised capacity always halve the download time?

Show the explanation

No. That conclusion assumes the link is the only limit and the full rate is available. The server, wireless connection or another part of the route may limit the transfer.

Try a small change: Calculate the ideal time for 120 megabits at 20 megabits per second, then name one reason a measured transfer might take longer.

Visual walkthrough

Separate three performance ideas

“The network is slow” is a starting observation. These terms describe different things to investigate.

Pause and predict: A remote service is overloaded. Will replacing a local switch necessarily speed up the download?

Show the explanation

No. The limiting resource may be the remote service, so changing the local switch may not affect it. Use evidence to identify the bottleneck first.

Practice and explain

Explain

Does replacing a switch always make Internet downloads faster?

Show explained answer

No. The Internet connection, wireless airtime or remote service may be the bottleneck. Measure or identify the constraint before recommending equipment.

Protect

Why should students not share an administrator account?

Show explained answer

Shared administration gives unnecessary privileges and weakens accountability. Individual accounts with limited permissions reduce unauthorised changes.

Your practical task

Plan a school lab with 20 wired computers, 10 wireless laptops, a file server and Internet access. Draw the logical network and make an addressing table. Explain two security controls and two choices intended to improve performance.

Show illustrative answer / example

Connect wired clients and the file server to a switch, and connect an access point for laptops. Include routing to the provider and a firewall in the course diagram outside the trusted network. Use a labelled /24 private network and unique addresses. Restrict server permissions and update operating systems. Use wired links for stationary devices and assess access-point placement and concurrent wireless demand. Justify choices against the stated requirements; several designs may be valid.

Check your understanding

Which statement about a basic switch is correct?

It removes all broadcasts It forwards local frames but broadcasts still use network resources It replaces every router

Quick-check answer and explanation

It forwards local frames but broadcasts still use network resources

A basic switch forwards local frames. Broadcasts remain within the broadcast domain, while routers connect and separate IP networks.

Diagnose

A client has 192.168.40.12/24 but its gateway is 192.168.41.1. What should you check?

Show explained answer

The configured gateway is outside the client’s /24 local network. Check the intended addressing plan and set the correct reachable local gateway. Do not change settings on a real school network without the administrator.

A learner says “ping works, so the website must work”. Explain the error.

Calculate

In an idealised transfer, how long does 80 megabits take over a 20 megabit-per-second link?

Show explained answer

80 ÷ 20 = 4 seconds. This assumes the full rate is available and ignores overhead and delay. Megabits are not megabytes.

Your practical task

Try the library scenario before opening the illustrative answer. Compare your choices and reasoning with it. Note your corrections, then explain one mistake and why your revised answer is better.

Show illustrative answer / example

UNIT 1 / WEEK 9 / CHAPTER 10

Software, ownership and licensing

Before you copy or adapt code, check what its licence allows. Giving credit and having permission are separate responsibilities.

SOFTWARE RESPONSIBILITY CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Explain intellectual property, copyright, piracy and plagiarism.
  • Compare open-source and proprietary software licences.
  • Create a source record for reused code.

Before you start: Recognise source code and explain what you have written or reused.

Revisit if needed: Designing and testing solutions.

Find this chapter’s activities and downloads.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. Ideas, expression and permissions

Copying someone’s program and giving them credit does not automatically make the copying permitted. You need to check both who created the work and what you are allowed to do with it.

Copyright protects original expression, including computer programs. It does not protect an abstract idea by itself. In Australia, protection generally starts automatically; registration is not required. The main law is the Copyright Act 1968.

Unauthorised copying or distribution of protected software is commonly called software piracy. Presenting another person’s work as your own is plagiarism. These are different issues: acknowledgement addresses authorship, while permission depends on the work and its licence. Source: Attorney-General’s Department: copyright basics.

2. Read the licence before reuse

Before reusing code, read its licence. It explains permitted uses and any conditions. A proprietary licence may allow you to use software while restricting access to its source or permission to redistribute it. Proprietary software may be paid or free of charge.

An open-source licence allows use, modification and redistribution under its conditions. You may need to keep notices, give attribution or share modified source under a compatible licence. Open source does not mean “no copyright”.

A public repository without a licence does not automatically grant open-source rights. A free download does not automatically permit changes or redistribution either. Compare the licences, rather than judging by price or where the software is hosted.

Definition reference: Open Source Initiative. For permissions, also consult Australian Government guidance for copyright users.

Visual walkthrough

Check two separate responsibilities

Giving credit and having permission answer different questions. Check both before reusing code.

Pause and predict: A tutorial is credited in your source log, but its licence does not allow redistribution. Does the credit solve that restriction?

Show the explanation

No. Credit addresses attribution; it does not override the licence. You need permission for the intended use and must follow its conditions.

Try a small change: Explain why an open-source licence can still have obligations. Name one example, such as keeping required copyright notices.

For each part you reuse:

  1. Record its creator, exact source and version.
  2. Read the licence and note its conditions.
  3. Keep the notices and acknowledgements the licence requires.
  4. Describe which part you used and what you changed.
  5. Follow any school rules about permitted assistance.

If the rights are unclear, write your own implementation or obtain appropriate permission.

Distinguish

1. Diagnose before choosing practice

Try the six prompts without opening the answers. For each one, record “secure”, “unsure” or “revisit”. If you guessed correctly, still check that you can explain why. Use the results to choose a practice station.

D1. Represent character B (decimal code point 66) in binary and hexadecimal.

Show explained answer

1000010 (or 01000010 for eight-bit notation), and 42 hexadecimal. The number is unchanged.

D2. Evaluate NOT False AND False OR True.

Show explained answer

True. NOT first gives True; AND then gives False; OR True gives True. Grouping it as NOT (False AND False OR True) would instead give False.

D3. Trace [4, 9, 9] through a first-maximum algorithm.

Show explained answer

Initial best index 0; after index 1 best is 1; after index 2 it stays 1. Strict comparison preserves the first tie.

D4. Choose a file mode that retains yesterday’s records.

Show explained answer

Append, a. Read does not add records; write replaces existing content.

D5. Are 192.168.6.10 and 192.168.7.10 local under /24?

Show explained answer

No. Networks are 192.168.6.0 and 192.168.7.0. Routing is required between them.

D6. Does crediting copied code make every reuse permissible?

Show explained answer

No. Check the licence or permission independently of attribution.

2. Station A: Boolean expressions and types

A visitor can enter if they are at least 16 and have permission, or if they are escorted. Write (age >= 16 and has_permission) or is_escorted. Then translate and and or to uppercase pseudocode operators.

Test ages 15, 16 and 17. For each age, try permission true and false, and escorted true and false. At age 15 with permission True and escorted False, admission is False. Change only escorted to True: admission becomes True. Explain which part of the condition changed the decision.

Compare not (a and b) with (not a) and b using a=False and b=False. The results are True and False. Choose a type for each value too: an integer item count, a float measured length, a string identifier such as “0042”, and Boolean permission. Explain why each type fits.

3. Types, operators and functions together

This original pair applies integer age, float length, string LABEL and Boolean permission. Trace the arguments into the parameters; the local admitted value is returned. The global constant LABEL is read, not changed. Predict Visitor 1.5 True followed by True.

Pseudocode

CONST LABEL = "Visitor"
FUNCTION Describe(age, length, has_permission)
    admitted = age >= 16 AND has_permission
    PRINT(LABEL, length, admitted)
    RETURN admitted
END Describe
PRINT(Describe(16, 1.5, TRUE))

Python

LABEL = "Visitor"
def describe(age, length, has_permission):
    admitted = age >= 16 and has_permission
    print(LABEL, length, admitted)
    return admitted
print(describe(16, 1.5, True))

Compare 2 == 2 (True), 2 != 2 (False), 2 > 2 (False), 2 < 2 (False), 2 >= 2 (True) and 2 <= 2 (True). Change one operand and predict again. Translate Python and/or/not to AND/OR/NOT in your algorithm.

4. Station B: algorithms in two representations

Write the steps and trace them before coding. In this pseudocode, = assigns and == compares. Structural keywords are uppercase and each block has an ending. The FOR bounds include both ends. In these positive-step examples, a start above the finish gives zero passes.

FUNCTION LoadAndShow
    values = []
    value = 0
    FOR i = 0 TO 3
        INPUT(value)
        values.append(value)
    END FOR
    FOR i = 0 TO values.length - 1
        PRINT(i, values[i])
    END FOR
END LoadAndShow
FUNCTION Total(values)
    total = 0
    FOR i = 0 TO values.length - 1
        total = total + values[i]
    END FOR
    RETURN total
END Total
FUNCTION FirstMaximum(values)
    best = -1
    IF values.length > 0 THEN
        best = 0
        FOR i = 1 TO values.length - 1
            IF values[i] > values[best] THEN
                best = i
            END IF
        END FOR
    END IF
    RETURN best
END FirstMaximum

To find a minimum, reverse the comparison to <. FirstMaximum returns -1 for an empty array. Check this result before indexing: in Python, index -1 means the last element, not “not found”.

Translate the algorithms into Python. Test an empty list, one value, all-negative values and repeated minimum or maximum values. The load task assumes four valid integer inputs. Add validation as a separate extension.

5. Station C: debug and prove the correction

A maximum algorithm starts best_value at zero. Try [-8, -3]. It may incorrectly keep zero, even though zero is not in the list. After checking that the list is not empty, start from its first value instead.

Reproduce the failure, then follow the changing values. Temporary print statements can show which branches run and the current index and best value. Fix the cause and rerun both the failed test and earlier tests. Remove the diagnostic prints when finished.

Name the kind of error: a missing colon is a syntax error; an invalid index causes a runtime error; a wrong comparison may cause a logic error.

Visual walkthrough

Find the first wrong value

A faulty maximum search starts its largest value at 0 and checks [-8, -3]. Neither item is larger than 0.

Pause and predict: Why might testing only [4, 9, 9] fail to expose this zero-start bug?

Show the explanation

A positive value replaces zero, so that test can still find the correct maximum. All-negative data exposes the incorrect starting value.

Try a small change: Explain which extra cases check different risks: an empty list, a one-element list and repeated largest values.

Read three quantity records 2, 0 and 5 and predict a total of 7. In a practice folder, create the file in write mode, process it in read mode, then append 3 and check the new total 10. Use with statements to ensure files are closed, and document how missing or malformed files are handled.

Review one club-project requirement with its actual test result. Explain a unit test, an organiser acceptance trial and a developer retrospective. Add an API example and your source log. A proposed expected output is a plan; an observed comparison is test evidence.

Pause and predict

Can a mean be computed from no observations?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download mean_without_zero_division.py

def mean(values):
    if len(values) == 0:
        return None
    total = 0
    for value in values:
        total += value
    return total / len(values)
for values in [[], [0], [10, 20]]:
    print(values, mean(values))
Show expected output after your prediction
[] None
[0] 0.0
[10, 20] 15.0

2. Q1

Character C has decimal code point 67. Write its binary and hexadecimal values, then explain whether a code point always occupies one byte.

Show explained answer

1000011 or 01000011. hexadecimal 43. a code point identifies a character; byte length depends on encoding, so it is not always one byte.

3. Q2

Show explained answer

remainder 3. Boolean result True. ((not False) and False) or True, with NOT before AND before OR. = assigns; == compares.

4. Q3

Given values = [6, -2, 6], trace a first-maximum algorithm initialised with best = 0 and updated only when values[i] > values[best]. State the final index, maximum and sum. Explain the empty-array precaution.

Show explained answer

at i=1, best remains 0. at i=2, best remains 0 because 6 > 6 is false. index 0 and maximum 6. sum 10. check non-empty before accessing element zero; define an empty result. Other clear trace layouts are possible.

5. Q4

Write a Python function admission(age, has_permission, is_escorted) returning (age >= 16 and has_permission) or is_escorted. Identify parameters and the arguments in admission(15, True, False), and give the result.

Show explained answer

valid function header with the three parameters. correctly grouped return expression. age/has_permission/is_escorted are parameters; 15/True/False are arguments. False.

6. Q5

A score must be a whole number from 0 to 100 inclusive. Give below/at/above tests for the upper boundary, a conversion-failure input, and state expected outcomes.

Show explained answer

99 accepted. 100 accepted. 101 rejected. text such as abc or 2.5 rejected as integer input. State the expected outcome alongside each input.

7. Q6

Yesterday’s file contains one line 2. A program adds today’s quantity 3 using w mode. Explain the failure, select the correct mode, explain reliable closure, and predict the sum after the corrected append-and-read operation.

Show explained answer

w replaces the earlier data. use a to retain and append, with a newline record separator. a with block closes the file when the block exits. sum 5 after reading the two records; assume valid integer lines.

8. Q7

A project has a correct calculation but users cannot recover from an invalid quantity. Explain why it is incomplete, propose acceptance evidence, identify a unit test and describe a useful retrospective point.

Show explained answer

it fails an agreed recovery requirement despite correct calculation. organiser enters invalid text then a valid quantity and continues without restarting. isolated calculation call with known input and expected return. evidence-based reflection about the development process and a future change, such as earlier validation testing.

9. Q8

A public repository has visible source but no licence. Explain why visibility alone does not establish open-source status; distinguish plagiarism from copyright permission; name one item to record before reusing code.

Show explained answer

open source requires licence rights to use, modify and redistribute, not just visibility. plagiarism concerns misrepresenting authorship; acknowledgement does not independently grant permission. exact licence/permission and conditions, or creator/source/version with an explanation of its use.

10. Q9

For a protected web request using TCP, name the four DoD TCP/IP layers in order and give one responsibility or suitable protocol at each.

Show explained answer

Application — HTTPS/web service; Transport — TCP/ordered stream; Internet — IP/addressing and routing; Network — Ethernet or Wi-Fi/local frames. Explain both the layer and its role or example.

11. Q10

Compare IPv4 with IPv6. Are 192.168.8.10 and 192.168.9.10 local to each other under 255.255.255.0? Explain the mask’s role.

Show explained answer

IPv4 32 bits versus IPv6 128 bits (IPv6 has a larger address space). no, their /24 network addresses differ. the mask identifies the network portion used in that comparison.

12. Q11

Draw a logical diagram for eight wired PCs, six wireless laptops, a local server and Internet access. Use course Cisco-style conventions; include required addresses/masks and security. Justify one medium and one performance decision.

Show explained answer

switch with wired PCs and local server. access point links wireless clients to the LAN. router and appropriate provider/modem connection, with correctly connected course symbols. coherent unique addresses/masks and firewall outside trusted network without IP label. justified medium, such as UTP for fixed nearby PCs or fibre for a suitably described long link. evidence-based performance choice, such as investigating wireless airtime/placement rather than assuming a faster switch fixes everything. Teacher visually checks symbol fidelity; other coherent layouts are possible.

13. Q12

Explain how a firewall and an operating system help prevent unauthorised access. Explain why broadcasts and shared-medium contention can affect performance.

Show explained answer

firewall permits/blocks traffic according to rules. OS authentication, permissions or updates with a threat explanation. broadcasts consume capacity/processing within the broadcast domain. contention/collisions on shared media consume time; modern full-duplex switched Ethernet avoids old half-duplex collision behaviour.

14. Turn feedback into a plan

Check one point at a time using the explained answers. Equivalent correct explanations and working are acceptable. For each mistake, decide whether you needed more knowledge, made a tracing/calculation error, misread the question or did not explain your reasoning clearly.

Choose your three weakest questions. Change the data, try again and explain what you corrected. Written answers do not replace practical work. You still need opportunities to load arrays, process files, develop and debug programs, keep development records and draw LAN, WLAN and WAN diagrams. Use the coverage audit to see what remains to be checked.

Use a mistake to choose the next practice

The useful result of practice is knowing what to work on next. Keep the correction small and specific.

Pause and predict: You copied a correct answer but cannot explain why it works. What should you do before moving on?

Show the explanation

Revisit the idea, explain the reasoning without copying, then try a changed example and check it. Copying alone does not show understanding.

Try a small change: Return to one topic after a break. Cover your notes, write the main idea and an example from memory, then check and correct them.

15. Explain a trace rather than memorise output

Use the example as a worked model, then fade the support: predict on paper, trace one execution together, change one requirement and test independently. The code is ordinary Python 3 and runs offline. Work in a disposable learning folder. These are ungraded practice examples, not additional assessment requirements.

Record the input or initial state, expected outcome, actual outcome, pass/fail and a reason. Where an invalid input is outside the function's stated contract, explain that precondition rather than silently inventing behaviour.

Pause and predict

Which result changes in the caller, and which name is unavailable outside its function?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download scope_and_return.py

score = 10
def add_bonus(current, bonus):
    updated = current + bonus
    return updated
result = add_bonus(score, 5)
print(score, result)
# updated belongs to the call, not the module's namespace.
try:
    print(updated)
except NameError:
    print("updated is local")
def broken_bonus():
    score = score + 5
    return score
try:
    broken_bonus()
except UnboundLocalError:
    print("local score read before assignment")
Show expected output after your prediction
10 15
updated is local
local score read before assignment

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Cover the output and produce a two-scope trace before checking the guide.
  2. Independent transfer: Create one new normal case, one boundary/empty case and one missing/invalid case relevant to this example. State any preconditions. Predict independently, run, explain the first mismatch if present, and keep the cases for regression after your change.
  3. Delayed retrieval: After a gap, solve a changed version without copying the example. Explain one design decision and use a new test to demonstrate transfer.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The module score is 10 and returned result is 15. State which name is bound in which scope; a return does not export every local name.

16. Check your reasoning, test the claim and retain the evidence

Use the cases below as starting points, not a complete test plan. Write the expected outcome before running code, issuing SQL or revealing the explanation. For a conceptual claim, use the scenario and a counterexample; for implemented behaviour, record observed results. If the school has not run a check, label it pending.

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Complete the first case with teacher modelling, the second with a partner, then swap explanations and challenge one assumption.
  2. Independent transfer: Create a third case that could expose an error the first two would miss. Record the expected and actual evidence, explain any mismatch, repair one cause and repeat both the new case and earlier cases.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Return after another topic and attempt a changed case without viewing the worked explanation. Explain what transferred and what still needs support.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The expected-evidence column gives the starting reference. A sound check explains the rule and its limits, not only a pass label. Keep a contrary or invalid case when appropriate, plus an unaffected case after a change. Your own actual-result evidence is still required.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Lesson 1: reading and first paper attempt; continue in lesson 2 if needed.
  2. Lesson 2: finish the attempt, then check using the explanations.
  3. Lesson 3: fresh questions and teacher feedback on weak areas.
  4. Lesson 4: final retrieval, diagram/trace checks and a personal exam plan. Weeks 17–18 remain blocked for exams.
